{{Short description|Second-smallest eigenvalue of a graph Laplacian}}
[[Image:6n-graf.svg|thumb|250px|An example graph, with 6 vertices, [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]] 3, [[connectivity (graph theory)|connectivity]] 1, and algebraic connectivity 0.722]]
The '''algebraic connectivity''' (also known as '''Fiedler value''' or '''Fiedler eigenvalue''' after [[Miroslav Fiedler]]) of a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] ''{{Mvar|G}}'' is the second-smallest [[eigenvalue]] (counting multiple eigenvalues separately) of the [[Laplacian matrix]] of ''{{Mvar|G}}''.<ref>Weisstein, Eric W. "[http://mathworld.wolfram.com/AlgebraicConnectivity.html Algebraic Connectivity]." From MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource.</ref> This eigenvalue is greater than 0 if and only if ''{{Mvar|G}}'' is a [[connected graph]]. This is a corollary to the fact that the number of times 0 appears as an eigenvalue in the Laplacian is the number of connected components in the graph. The magnitude of this value reflects how well connected the overall graph is. It has been used in analyzing the robustness and [[synchronizability]] of networks.

== Properties ==
[[file:C60 Molecule.svg|thumb|The [[truncated icosahedron]] or [[Buckminsterfullerene]] graph has a traditional [[connectivity (graph theory)|connectivity]] of 3, and an algebraic connectivity of 0.243.]]
The algebraic connectivity of undirected graphs with nonnegative weights is <math>a(G)\geq0</math>, with the inequality being strict if and only if {{Mvar|G}} is connected. However, the algebraic connectivity can be negative for general directed graphs, even if ''{{Mvar|G}}'' is a [[connected graph]].<ref name="wu2004">{{cite journal|author-last=Wu|author-first=Chai Wai| title=Algebraic connectivity of directed graphs| year=2005|volume=53|number=3|pages=203–223|doi=10.1080/03081080500054810| journal=Linear and Multilinear Algebra | publisher=[[Taylor and Francis]]|s2cid=121368189 | quote=Even if G is quasi-strongly connected, which is equivalent to G containing a directed spanning tree, a(G) can still be nonpositive as the exploding star and Theorem 1 indicate.}}</ref> Furthermore, the value of the algebraic connectivity is bounded above by the traditional (vertex) [[connectivity (graph theory)|connectivity]] of a graph, <math>\text{algebraic connectivity} \le \text{connectivity}</math>, unless the graph is complete (the algebraic connectivity of a [[complete graph]] {{mvar|K{{sub|n}}}} is its order {{mvar|n}}).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fiedler |first=Miroslav |date=1973 |title=Algebraic connectivity of graphs |url=https://dml.cz/handle/10338.dmlcz/101168 |journal=Czechoslovak Mathematical Journal |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=298–305 |doi=10.21136/cmj.1973.101168 |issn=0011-4642|hdl=10338.dmlcz/101168 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> For an undirected connected graph with nonnegative edge weights, ''{{mvar|n}}'' vertices, and [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]] ''{{Mvar|D}}'', the algebraic connectivity is also known to be bounded below by <math display="inline">\frac{1}{nD} </math>,<ref>{{cite book |editor1-first=J.L. |editor1-last=Gross |editor2-first=J. |editor2-last=Yellen |title=Handbook of Graph Theory |publisher=CRC Press |date=2004 |page=571 |isbn=0-203-49020-7 |doi=10.1201/b16132 |hdl=2117/22000 }}</ref> and in fact (in a result due to [[Brendan McKay (mathematician)|Brendan McKay]]) by <math display="inline">\frac{4}{nD}</math>.<ref name="Mohar">{{cite conference |author-link=Bojan Mohar |first=Bojan |last=Mohar |url=http://www.fmf.uni-lj.si/~mohar/Papers/Spec.pdf |title=The Laplacian Spectrum of Graphs |zbl=0840.05059  |book-title=Graph Theory, Combinatorics, and Applications. Proceedings of the sixth quadrennial international conference on the theory and applications of graphs |volume=2 |editor1-first=Y. |editor1-last=Alavi |editor2-first=G. |editor2-last=Chartrand |editor3-link=Ortrud Oellermann |editor3-first=O.R. |editor3-last=Oellermann |editor4-first=A.J. |editor4-last=Schwenk |publisher=Wiley |date=1991 |pages=871–898}}</ref> For the example graph with 6 nodes show above (<math display="inline">n=6, D=3</math>), these bounds would be calculated as:<math display="block">4/18 = 0.222 \le \text{algebraic connectivity 0.722} \le \text{connectivity 1.} </math>Unlike the [[k-vertex-connected graph|traditional form of graph connectivity]], defined by local configurations whose removal would disconnect the graph, the algebraic connectivity is dependent on the global number of vertices, as well as the way in which vertices are connected. In [[random graph]]s, the algebraic connectivity decreases with the number of vertices, and increases with the average [[degree (graph theory)|degree]].<ref>{{cite conference |last=Holroyd |first=Michael |date=2006 |title=Synchronization and Connectivity of Discrete Complex Systems |url=https://meekohi.com/Holroyd06/ |conference= |book-title=International Conference on Complex Systems}}</ref>

The exact definition of the algebraic connectivity depends on the type of Laplacian used. [[Fan Chung]] has developed an extensive theory using a rescaled version of the Laplacian, eliminating the dependence on the number of vertices, so that the bounds are somewhat different.<ref>{{cite book |first=F.R.K. |last=Chung |title=Spectral Graph Theory |publisher=Amer. Math. Soc. |date=1997 |isbn=0-8218-8936-2 |url={{GBurl|YUc38_MCuhAC|pg=PP1}} |series=Regional Conference Series in Mathematics |volume=92}} [http://www.math.ucsd.edu/~fan/research/revised.html Incomplete revised edition]</ref>

In models of [[synchronization]] on networks, such as the [[Kuramoto model]], the Laplacian matrix arises naturally, so the algebraic connectivity gives an indication of how easily the network will synchronize.<ref>{{cite arXiv |first=Tiago |last=Pereira |eprint=1112.2297 |title=Stability of Synchronized Motion in Complex Networks |date=2011|class=nlin.AO }}</ref> Other measures, such as the average [[distance (graph theory)|distance]] (characteristic path length) can also be used,<ref>{{cite book |first=D. |last=Watts |title=Six Degrees: The Science of a Connected Age |publisher=Vintage |date=2003 |isbn=0-434-00908-3 |oclc=51622138}}</ref> and in fact the algebraic connectivity is closely related to the (reciprocal of the) average distance.<ref name="Mohar" />

The algebraic connectivity also relates to other connectivity attributes, such as the [[isoperimetric number]], which is bounded below by half the algebraic connectivity.<ref>{{cite book |first=Norman |last=Biggs |title=Algebraic Graph Theory |edition=2nd |publisher=Cambridge University Press |date=1993 |pages=28, 58  |isbn=0-521-45897-8 |url={{GBurl|6TasRmIFOxQC|p=58}}}}</ref>

== Fiedler vector ==
The original theory related to algebraic connectivity was produced by [[Miroslav Fiedler]].<ref>{{cite journal |first=M. |last=Fiedler |title=Algebraic connectivity of Graphs |journal=Czechoslovak Mathematical Journal |volume=23 |issue=98 |date=1973 |pages=298–305 |doi=10.21136/CMJ.1973.101168 |zbl=0265.05119 |mr=0318007|doi-access=free |hdl=10338.dmlcz/101168 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first=M. |last=Fiedler |title=Laplacian of graphs and algebraic connectivity  |orig-date=1987 |journal=Banach Center Publications |volume=25 |issue=1 |date=1989 |pages=57–70 |doi=10.4064/-25-1-57-70 |url=https://www.infona.pl/resource/bwmeta1.element.zamlynska-edcb2a23-d1dd-4cf0-9758-88e7498fc81e/content/partDownload/2c2bb783-deff-3703-ad86-9747846992a6
|doi-access=free }}</ref> In his honor the [[eigenvector]] associated with the algebraic connectivity has been named the '''Fiedler vector'''. The Fiedler vector can be used to [[graph partition|partition]] a graph. 

=== Partitioning a graph using the Fiedler vector === 
[[File:6n-graf2.svg|thumb|Partitioning into two connected graphs]]
For the example graph in the introductory section, the Fiedler vector is <math display="inline"> \begin{pmatrix} 0.415 & 0.309 & 0.069 & -0.221 & 0.221 & -0.794 \end{pmatrix} </math>. The negative values are associated with the poorly connected vertex 6, and the neighbouring [[articulation point]], vertex 4; while the positive values are associated with the other vertices. The signs of the values in the Fiedler vector can therefore be used to partition this graph into two components: <math display="inline"> \{ 1, 2, 3, 5 \}, \{ 4, 6 \} </math>. Alternatively, the value of 0.069 (which is close to zero) can be placed in a class of its own, partitioning the graph into three components: <math display="inline"> \{ 1, 2, 5 \}, \{ 3 \} , \{ 4, 6 \} </math> or moved to the other partition <math display="inline"> \{ 1, 2, 5 \}, \{ 3, 4, 6 \} </math>, as pictured. The squared values of the components of the Fiedler vector, summing up to one since the vector is normalized, can be interpreted as probabilities of the corresponding data points to be assigned to the sign-based partition.
